opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons. The most straightforward one is just compute. If you look at 2024, there wasn't really a big jump in the scale of the largest training runs compared to where we were with GPT-4. Most of what we saw in 2024 were models at roughly that same compute scale, made more efficient, cheaper, a bit better through algorithmic improvements and better post-training. But we didn't see the next order-of-magnitude scale-up land. The labs have been building out much larger clusters, the 100,000-GPU-scale clusters, and the models trained on those should start coming out in 2025. So I expect a bigger step there than we got last year.

The second reason is the reasoning paradigm, the o1 and o3 style of models, where you use reinforcement learning to train the model to think for longer before answering. That's a new axis we're really only at the beginning of. When you have a fresh paradigm like that, the early gains tend to come quickly, because there's a lot of low-hanging fruit. You can scale up the RL compute, scale up the inference compute, and get big jumps on things like math and coding benchmarks in a matter of months. The jump from o1 to o3 already showed how fast that can move.

And third, these two things compound. Better base models from the larger pretraining runs give you a better starting point for the reinforcement learning, and the reasoning training then extracts more out of them. So you get the pretraining scale-up and the new post-training paradigm arriving at roughly the same time.

I'd add one caveat: I don't think faster progress on benchmarks automatically means we get very general, autonomous agents that can do long, open-ended tasks reliably. That's a harder problem, and I'd be more cautious there. But in terms of raw capability gains, especially in domains with clear feedback like math and programming, I'd expect 2025 to look noticeably faster than 2024.

r001.rationale: The response names compute as its most straightforward reason and expects a larger step in 2025 as much larger training clusters begin producing models.

r002.rationale: It identifies scaling reinforcement-learning compute and inference compute for reasoning models as additional progress avenues beyond larger pretraining runs.

r003.rationale: It discusses a coming scale-up and rapid reasoning gains, but does not say that each order-of-magnitude increase has a good chance of unlocking a new capability.

r004.rationale: It mentions 100,000-GPU-scale clusters coming online, but does not identify them as H100 clusters.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that the inputs to AI progress are growing faster now than they were a year or two ago. If you look at what actually drives capabilities, it's mostly compute, and then on top of that, algorithmic improvements, and then the data you're able to use. And on the compute side, the amount of compute being spent on frontier training runs has been growing at something like four or five times per year for a while now. That's a very fast rate. But what's changed recently is that the amount of capital being committed has accelerated even beyond that trend. The hyperscalers are spending enormous amounts on data centers, the chip supply is expanding, and so the compute that's going to be available in 2025 for training and, importantly, for inference, is substantially more than what was available in 2024.

The second thing is that we've seen a new direction of scaling open up with reasoning models, things like o1 and o3. Before, most of the gains came from scaling pretraining, which was starting to look like it was running into some constraints, partly data, partly just that the models were getting very expensive to train. But now you have this additional axis where you can spend compute at inference time, and you can train models with reinforcement learning to use that inference compute productively. And that's a pretty immature technique right now. When a technique is immature, you tend to get very rapid gains from scaling it up, because you're picking the low-hanging fruit. So I'd expect that in 2025, we'll see much larger reinforcement learning runs, much more inference-time compute being used, and that will produce gains that look faster than the pretraining-only gains we were seeing in 2024.

And then the third thing, which is more speculative, is that the models themselves are getting good enough to start contributing to the research process in small ways. I don't mean full automation of AI research, I think we're quite far from that. But things like writing code, running experiments, helping with the engineering work, that's starting to be useful. And if the labs can get even modest productivity gains from that, it compounds with the other effects.

So you put those together, more compute, a new and immature scaling paradigm, and some early automation of the labor going into research, and I think it's reasonable to expect the pace of progress in 2025 to be noticeably faster than what we saw in 2024. I'd put some caveats on that, of course. There's always uncertainty about whether a paradigm keeps scaling, and 2024 itself felt a bit slow to some people, so part of this is also just a correction from that. But on net, I'd expect it to be faster.

r001.rationale: The response says faster progress comes from three factors together: more compute, a new reasoning-scaling paradigm, and early research automation. It does not clearly make increased compute scaling the primary cause.

r002.rationale: It identifies inference-time compute and reinforcement learning for reasoning models as a new scaling axis beyond pretraining.

r003.rationale: It does not say that each order-of-magnitude increase in scale has a good chance of unlocking a new capability.

r004.rationale: It mentions expanding chip supply and data-center investment, but does not attribute compute growth to large H100 clusters coming online.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that the investments made over the last couple of years are still working their way through to actual capabilities. Spending money on compute doesn't immediately produce a better model. You have to build the infrastructure, run the training, and then do the work needed to turn that model into something useful. So progress in 2024 doesn't necessarily tell you how much progress to expect in 2025.

There's also another avenue for improvement, which is letting models spend more compute working on a problem before answering. That means progress doesn't depend exclusively on making the next pretraining run bigger. You can also improve how models reason, how they're trained to use that extra computation, and how much computation you give them at inference time.

So my expectation is that we'll see improvements from both directions. But I'd distinguish that from saying we're guaranteed some dramatic breakthrough in 2025. The timing of individual releases is quite noisy, and a calendar year is a fairly arbitrary window over which to measure progress.

r001.rationale: The response cites ongoing investments and compute spending, but presents pretraining and inference-time computation as two directions without making increased compute scaling the primary reason.

r002.rationale: It identifies giving models more computation before answering, and improving their use of that computation, as an avenue beyond making pretraining runs bigger.

r003.rationale: It does not say that each order-of-magnitude increase in scale has a good chance of unlocking a new capability.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute greater compute scaling in 2025 to large H100 clusters coming online.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that there’s a lag between investing in AI and seeing the resulting capabilities. You need to build the infrastructure, run experiments, train models, and then turn those models into products. So some of the investment and research activity in 2024 should show up as progress in 2025.

There’s also a relatively new direction for scaling: giving models more computation when they’re answering a question. Instead of relying entirely on a larger training run, you can let a model spend more time working through a problem and checking its answer. That gives us another way to improve performance, particularly on tasks where you can verify whether an answer is correct.

I wouldn’t say faster progress is guaranteed. But with more resources going into training, and more room to explore how models use computation at inference time, I think there are good reasons to expect it.

r001.rationale: The candidate mainly credits a lag between AI investment and visible progress. It mentions more training resources and inference-time computation, but does not attribute the expectation primarily to increased compute scaling.

r002.rationale: It describes giving models more computation while answering questions as another way to improve performance beyond relying on a larger training run.

r003.rationale: It does not mention order-of-magnitude increases in scale or the chance that each could unlock a new capability.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute greater compute scaling to large H100 clusters coming online.
